title: Single-Slit Fraunhofer Diffraction
short_intro: Single-slit diffraction is the bending and interference of light waves when passing through a single aperture of comparable dimensions to the light's wavelength. It produces a central bright maximum flanked by alternating secondary minima and smaller maxima.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Qualitative understanding of diffraction, conditions for minima and maxima, width of the central maximum, and distinction between interference and diffraction.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Quantitative derivation of intensity distribution using phasor addition, path and phase difference calculations, angular width, and resolving power applications.

concept_notes.heading: Physical Origin of Single-Slit Diffraction
bullets: Every point on the wavefront within the slit of width a acts as a source of secondary wavelet disturbances.
The resultant displacement at any point on the screen is the superposition of all wavelets traveling in a given direction θ.
Destructive interference occurs when wavelets from different parts of the slit cancel each other out completely due to path differences.

concept_notes.heading: Condition for Minima (Dark Fringes)
bullets: Minima are formed on the screen when the path difference between waves from the top and bottom edges of the slit equals an integral multiple of the wavelength.
Mathematically expressed as a sin θ = nλ, where n = ±1, ±2, ±3, ...
The integer n = 0 corresponds to the central maximum, not a minimum.

concept_notes.heading: Condition for Secondary Maxima (Bright Fringes)
bullets: Secondary maxima occur approximately halfway between the diffraction minima.
The condition for secondary maxima is given by a sin θ = (n + 0.5)λ, where n = ±1, ±2, ±3, ...
The intensity of secondary maxima decreases rapidly as the diffraction angle θ increases away from the central axis.

concept_notes.heading: Intensity Distribution
bullets: The intensity I at any angle θ is given by I = I0 (sin β / β)2, where β = (πa / λ) sin θ.
The central maximum contains the vast majority of the total incident optical energy.
The angular half-width of the central maximum is defined by the angular position of the first minimum: θ ≈ λ / a.

derivations.title: Derivation of Minima Condition
derivations.conditions: Fraunhofer diffraction approximation, plane wavefront incident normally on a single slit of width a.
steps: Divide the slit of width a into two equal halves of width a/2.
The path difference between secondary wavelets originating from corresponding points in the upper and lower halves separated by a/2 is (a/2) sin θ.
Complete destructive interference between these two halves occurs when their path difference is half a wavelength: (a/2) sin θ = λ / 2.
Generalizing this subdivision for 2n zones leads to the condition a sin θ = nλ for n = ±1, ±2, ±3, ...

derivations.title: Derivation of Intensity Distribution
derivations.conditions: Integration of infinitesimal phasor amplitudes across the slit width a.
steps: Consider the slit divided into N infinitesimal strips, each of width dy. The amplitude contribution from each strip is dE = (E0 / a) dy.
The phase difference between the wave from element y and the center of the slit is dφ = (2π / λ) y sin θ.
Integrate the resultant electric field amplitude E(θ) across the slit from -a/2 to +a/2.
E(θ) = ∫-a/2a/2 (E0 / a) exp[i(2π/λ)y sin θ] dy, which evaluates to E0 (sin β / β) where β = (πa/λ) sin θ.
Since intensity I is proportional to the square of the amplitude (E), I(θ) = I0 (sin β / β)2.

formula_sheet.name: Condition for Diffraction Minima

formula_sheet.units: m for a and λ; radians or degrees for θ; dimensionless for n

formula_sheet.variables: a = slit width, θ = diffraction angle, n = integer order, λ = wavelength
formula_sheet.units: m for a and λ; radians for θ

formula_sheet.variables: I = intensity at angle θ, I_0 = intensity at central maximum, β = phase parameter (πa sin θ / λ)
formula_sheet.units: W/m<sup>2</sup> for I and I_0; dimensionless for β

formula_sheet.variables: θ<sub>1</sub> = angular position of first dark fringe, λ = wavelength, a = slit width

graphs_and_experiments.title: Intensity vs. Diffraction Angle Graph
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A central intense peak at θ = 0 with height I_0, flanked symmetrically by diminishing secondary peaks situated between minima located at θ = ±λ/a, ±2λ/a, etc.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Shows rapid drop in intensity away from the center; secondary maxima are much dimmer than the central peak (approx 4.5% for the first side maximum).
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Directly tested in questions asking for the sketch of the diffraction pattern or identification of secondary maxima positions.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Slit Width Variation Experiment
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Comparative sketches showing how narrowing slit width 'a' widens the diffraction pattern, while broadening 'a' compresses the pattern.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Inversely proportional relationship between slit width and angular spread (θ ∝ 1/a).
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Conceptual MCQs testing the effect of altering wavelength or slit width on fringe spacing and central maximum breadth.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Monochromatic vs White Light Diffraction Setup
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A schematic diagram showing a laser or monochromatic source versus a white light source forming a central white fringe with colored diffraction spectra on sides.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Different wavelengths diffract by different angles (since θ ∝ λ), causing red light to bend outward more than violet light.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Explaining the appearance of colored bands in white light single-slit experiments.

solved_numericals.question: Light of wavelength 500 nm falls normally on a single slit of width 0.2 mm. Calculate the angular position of the first secondary minimum in radians.
solution_steps: Identify given values: λ = 500 nm = 500 × 10<sup>-9</sup> m, a = 0.2 mm = 0.2 × 10<sup>-3</sup> m, n = 1.
Apply the diffraction minimum formula: a sin θ = nλ.

solved_numericals.question: A single slit of width 0.10 mm is illuminated by a parallel beam of light of wavelength 600 nm. The diffraction pattern is observed on a screen placed 2.0 m away. Calculate the linear width of the central maximum.
solution_steps: Identify given parameters: a = 0.10 mm = 1.0 × 10<sup>-4</sup> m, λ = 600 nm = 6 × 10<sup>-7</sup> m, D = 2.0 m.
Recall the formula for linear width of the central maximum: W = 2λD / a.
Substitute the given values into the equation: W = (2 × 6 × 10<sup>-7</sup> m × 2.0 m) / (1.0 × 10<sup>-4</sup> m).
Perform the multiplication in the numerator: 2 × 6 × 10<sup>-7</sup> × 2.0 = 2.4 × 10<sup>-6</sup>.
Divide by the denominator: W = 2.4 × 10<sup>-6</sup> / 1.0 × 10<sup>-4</sup> = 2.4 × 10<sup>-2</sup> m.

solved_numericals.question: At what angle does the first secondary maximum occur for a single slit of width 'a' illuminated by light of wavelength λ?
solution_steps: The secondary maxima occur approximately midway between the minima, governed by the condition: a sin θ = (n + 0.5)λ.
For the first secondary maximum, take n = 1.
Substitute n = 1 into the condition: a sin θ = (1 + 0.5)λ = 1.5λ = (3/2)λ.
Rearrange to solve for sin θ: sin θ = 3λ / (2a).

assumptions_and_limitations: Fraunhofer diffraction assumes both the source and the screen are effectively at an infinite distance from the slit, achieved experimentally using lenses.
The scalar wave approximation is used, ignoring polarization vector effects which become significant for sub-wavelength slit sizes.
The incident wavefront is treated as perfectly plane and parallel across the entire aperture.

common_misconceptions.wrong: The central maximum in single-slit diffraction has the same width and intensity as secondary maxima.
common_misconceptions.correct: The central maximum is twice as wide as any secondary maximum and contains significantly higher light intensity.
common_misconceptions.why: The central maximum spans from n = -1 to n = +1 (width 2λ/a), whereas secondary maxima lie between adjacent higher-order minima.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Diffraction minima correspond to points where light rays block each other out due to reflection.
common_misconceptions.correct: Minima occur due to complete destructive interference among secondary wavelets originating from different regions of the same single slit.
common_misconceptions.why: Destructive phase cancellation occurs when path differences cause phase opposition across the aperture wavefronts.

common_misconceptions.wrong: The formula a sin θ = nλ represents conditions for bright fringes in single-slit diffraction.
common_misconceptions.correct: In single-slit diffraction, a sin θ = nλ gives the positions of dark fringes (minima).
common_misconceptions.why: Students often confuse single-slit diffraction formulas with double-slit interference formulas, where nλ gives bright fringes.

quick_revision: Single slit dark fringe condition: a sin θ = nλ (n = 1, 2, 3...).
First secondary maximum position: a sin θ = 1.5λ.
Intensity of central maximum is proportional to E<sub>0</sub><sup>2</sup>, while side maxima drop off rapidly.
